title: Abu Hanifa
hook: the Kufa scholar and merchant, known for honesty and careful reasoning

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the foundations with ikhtilaf, and your line: difference, mercy. When someone read the same words differently, did you find their honest reading? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

A heap of grain sits in the market. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, walks past and pushes his hand into it, and his fingers come out wet. The top is dry. The damp is hidden underneath. Rain, the seller says. Then why not put the wet part on top, the Prophet asks, where people can see it? And then, in Sahih Muslim, the line: whoever cheats is not of me. A new part of this year begins today, with the schools of law, one by one. And it begins with a man who knew markets from the inside, because he earned his living in one.
screen: `A HEAP OF GRAIN, WET UNDERNEATH.` → `WHOEVER CHEATS IS NOT OF ME.` → `A SCHOLAR FROM THE MARKET.`

segments.voice: His name was al-Nu'man ibn Thabit, and he's remembered as Abu Hanifa. He lived in Kufa, in Iraq, a city full of scholars and full of trade, and he earned his living selling cloth. That detail matters. He wasn't a scholar who studied the market from a distance; he bought and sold, set prices, and dealt with customers who could be lied to. The biographies tell a story about it. Abu Hanifa gave his partner a garment to sell and told him it had a defect, and to point it out to the buyer. The partner sold it and forgot to mention it. When Abu Hanifa found out, the story goes, he gave away the whole price of that sale in charity, because he couldn't keep money from a sale that hid something. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari reads almost like a commentary on it: when buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their sale is blessed; when they hide and lie, the blessing is wiped away. Then the scholar. The biographies say Abu Hanifa taught in circles where students argued a question from every side before settling it. His method leaned on careful reasoning, and tomorrow we'll look at its tools. His students, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani among them, wrote down and carried the school that bears his name. A saying attributed to al-Shafi'i, founder of another school, calls people dependents of Abu Hanifa in law. The biographies also say he refused a post as a judge under the rulers of his time, and suffered for refusing. Hanafis call him al-Imam al-A'zam, the great imam. Honesty in the market, care in the argument: the school started with both.
screen: `AL-NU'MAN OF KUFA, A CLOTH MERCHANT.` · `THE GARMENT WITH A HIDDEN DEFECT.` · `TRUTHFUL AND CLEAR: A BLESSED SALE.` · `A CIRCLE THAT ARGUED EVERY SIDE.`

segments.voice: The practice: deal honestly in trade. Think of the next exchange you'll make: selling something online, splitting a bill, reporting your hours, returning something to a store. Where's the wet grain under the dry? A scratch you'd rather not mention. A minute you'd round up. Find it. Then picture yourself putting it on top, where the other person can see it. Notice what that costs, and what it frees. If you pray, you can ask for an honest hand. If not, hold that picture until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Abu Hanifa. Al-Nu'man ibn Thabit, cloth merchant and scholar of Kufa, after whom the Hanafi school is named. Today's word.
Your line: the great imam. Today, in one exchange, put the flaw on top where it can be seen, the way the market's scholar would. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Hanafi Muslims follow the school named for Abu Hanifa and carried by his students Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani, and Hanafis honor him with the title al-Imam al-A'zam, the great imam.
